question.text: Is laparoscopic adrenalectomy safe and effective for adrenal masses larger than 7 cm?
question.context: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy (LA) has become the gold standard treatment for small (less than 6 cm) adrenal masses. However, the role of LA for large-volume (more than 6 cm) masses has not been well defined. Our aim was to evaluate, retrospectively, the outcome of LA for adrenal lesions larger than 7 cm. 18 consecutive laparoscopic adrenalectomies were performed from 1996 to 2005 on patients with adrenal lesions larger than 7 cm. The mean tumor size was 8.3 cm (range 7-13 cm), the mean operative time was 137 min, the mean blood loss was 182 mL (range 100-550 mL), the rate of intraoperative complications was 16%, and in three cases we switched from laparoscopic procedure to open surgery.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The case describes a retrospective analysis of 18 laparoscopic adrenalectomies for lesions larger than 7 cm. The mean tumor size was 8.3 cm, and the mean operative time was 137 minutes. The rate of intraoperative complications was 16%, with three cases requiring conversion to open surgery. These findings suggest that laparoscopic adrenalectomy may not be safe or effective for large adrenal masses, as evidenced by the relatively high complication rate and conversion to open surgery.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The rate of intraoperative complications (16%) and the conversion to open surgery in three cases.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the case doesn't explicitly mention them, the differential diagnoses for adrenal masses include benign adenomas, adrenal carcinomas, and metastatic disease. However, the context of the case focuses on the safety and effectiveness of LA for large masses, and the findings suggest that LA may not be suitable for such cases.

These findings suggest that LA may be feasible but not without significant challenges, making 'maybe' the most cautious and evidence-based choice.

qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Open adrenalectomy was considered as an alternative due to complications; however, the study does not support LA as universally safe or effective for masses >7 cm, hence ruling out 'yes' or 'no' definitively.
